chunks.text:
This guide shows you how to run SightPress on your own computer, create your first website and sign in to its admin
panel, so that you can try it out. You don't need to know how to program. It takes about 30 minutes, most of which is
waiting for downloads.

!!! note "What you can try today"

    You can create a website with ready-made pages, write, schedule and publish pages, translate them into other
    languages, upload pictures and other files, invite people or let them sign up, make pages members-only, search
    the website, read its visitor statistics, turn features on or off, and set up an optional AI assistant with your
    own key. Running SightPress on a public server is not covered yet.

chunks.heading: What you need
chunks.text:
- A computer running Windows 10 or 11, macOS, or Linux.
- About 5 GB of free disk space.
- An internet connection.
- Permission to install programs on the computer.

You type some commands in a terminal. A terminal is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking:

- On Windows, open **Windows Terminal** or **PowerShell** from the Start menu.
- On macOS, open **Terminal** from Applications, then Utilities.
- On Linux, open your terminal app.

Type or paste each command, then press <kbd>Enter</kbd>.

chunks.heading: Step 1: install Docker
chunks.text:
Docker runs SightPress and everything it needs inside separate, self-contained boxes called containers. You don't
have to install PHP, a web server or a database yourself.

1. Install Docker:
    - On Windows or macOS, install [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/). On Windows, accept the
      option to use WSL 2 if the installer asks.
    - On Linux, install [Docker Engine and the Docker Compose plugin](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/).
2. On Windows or macOS, open Docker Desktop and wait until it says that Docker is running.
3. In the terminal, type:

    ```sh
    docker compose version
    ```

    You should see a line such as `Docker Compose version v5.3.0`. The number may be different. If you see
    "command not found" or a similar message, Docker is not installed correctly, or Docker Desktop is not running.

chunks.heading: Step 2: install Git
chunks.text:
Git downloads the SightPress files from GitHub, where they are published.

1. Install Git from the [Git downloads page](https://git-scm.com/downloads). On macOS, you can instead type
   `git --version` in the terminal and accept the offer to install the developer tools.
2. In the terminal, type:

    ```sh
    git --version
    ```

    You should see a line such as `git version 2.51.0`.

chunks.heading: Step 3: download SightPress
chunks.text:
You only download the `skeleton`, the project you start. The other parts of SightPress are fetched for you
automatically the first time you start it, in step 4.

1. Make a folder for SightPress and go into it:

    ```sh
    mkdir sightpress
    cd sightpress
    ```

2. Download the skeleton:

    ```sh
    git clone https://github.com/sightpress/skeleton.git
    ```

    You should see a few lines that end with `done.`

3. Go into the `skeleton` folder:

    ```sh
    cd skeleton
    ```

!!! tip "Only on Linux"

    The SightPress container writes files as user number 1000. If your Linux user has a different number, files
    can end up owned by the wrong user. Type `id -u`. If it shows anything other than `1000`, copy the settings
    file with `cp .env.example .env`, open `.env` in a text editor, and set `UID` and `GID` to the numbers that
    `id -u` and `id -g` show. Windows and macOS users can skip this.

chunks.heading: Step 4: start SightPress
chunks.text:
1. In the `skeleton` folder, type:

    ```sh
    docker compose up
    ```

2. Wait. The first time, Docker downloads and builds everything it needs. This can take 5 to 15 minutes. You see
   many lines of text scroll past. Later starts take a few seconds.
3. SightPress is ready when the text stops scrolling and you see lines starting with `php-1` that end with
   `ready to handle connections`.

Leave this terminal window open. SightPress stops when you close it.

chunks.heading: Step 5: open SightPress in your browser
chunks.text:
1. Open your web browser and go to <http://localhost:8080>.
2. You should see a plain page with the heading **No site configured** and this text: "SightPress is running, but
   no site is set up for this address yet. If you look after this server, create a site and link this address to
   it." The browser tab is called "No site configured - SightPress".

This is the right result. It means SightPress is running, but has no website yet. You create one in the next steps.

If the browser shows **502 Bad Gateway**, SightPress is still finishing its first start. Wait a minute, then
reload the page.

chunks.heading: Step 6: make a settings file with a secret key
chunks.text:
SightPress keeps its settings in a file called `.env` in the `skeleton` folder. One setting, the secret key, protects
the address of each website's database. You make it once.

1. Open a second terminal window and go to the `skeleton` folder, as in step 3. Leave the first window running.
2. Copy the example settings file:

    ```sh
    cp .env.example .env
    ```

3. Make a secret key:

    ```sh
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php php -r 'echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32)), PHP_EOL;'
    ```

    You should see one line of 64 letters and digits, such as `3f9a…`. Yours will be different.

4. Open the `.env` file in a text editor, such as Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on macOS. Find the line
   `APP_SECRET=` and paste your key straight after the `=` sign, with no spaces. Save the file.
5. Keep a copy of the key somewhere safe, such as a password manager. Without it, SightPress can't open your
   websites' databases.
6. Go back to the first terminal window and press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to stop SightPress. Then start it
   again with `docker compose up`, so that it reads the new settings.

The copied file also turns on the test e-mail inbox, which catches every e-mail SightPress sends. See
[Open the test e-mail inbox](how-to/open-the-test-email-inbox.md).

chunks.heading: Step 7: create your first website
chunks.text:
1. In the second terminal window, type this command on one line. Change the e-mail address and the names to your
   own if you like. (You can also type just `docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create` and
   answer one question at a time: see [Create a website](how-to/create-a-site.md).)

    ```sh
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create demo --domain=localhost --db=sqlite:////app/sites/demo.sqlite --url=http://localhost:8080 --owner-type=organization --locale=en-GB --name="Riverside Library" --admin-email=ada@example.org --admin-first-name=Ada --admin-last-name=Lovelace
    ```

2. After a few seconds, you should see lines like these:

    ```text
    Getting the SQLite file /app/sites/demo.sqlite ready…
    Ran 25 database migrations.
    Created the account of the first admin, Ada Lovelace (ada@example.org).
    Set up the roles admin, editor, contributor and member.
    Gave the first admin the admin role.
    Give the setup code 388 641 to ada@example.org. They go to http://localhost:8080/login/setup, type their email address and the code, and choose their password. The code works once, for 7 days.
    Made the site's icons, wordmark and share image from its name; replace them with site:branding:set.
    Published the starter pages in British English: Welcome to Riverside Library, About us, Contact us, Privacy notice, Terms of use, Accessibility statement.
    Added 5 starter pages to the main and footer menus.
    The

chunks.heading: Step 8: choose your password and sign in
chunks.text:
1. In your browser, go to <http://localhost:8080/login/setup>. You should see the heading **Set up your account**.
2. In **Email address**, type the address you used, for example `ada@example.org`.
3. In **6-digit code**, type the setup code. You can type it with or without the space.
4. Choose **Continue**. You should see the heading **Choose your password**.
5. In **New password**, type a password of at least 12 characters. A few unrelated words make a strong password
   that is easy to remember.
6. Choose **Set password**. You should see the sign-in page with the message "Your password has been set. Sign in
   with it now."
7. Type your e-mail address and your new password, then choose **Sign in**.
8. You should see the admin panel's **Dashboard**. The browser tab says "Dashboard - Admin - Riverside Library".
   The admin menu has links such as Dashboard, Pages, Analytics, Redirects, Media, Menus, People, Invite someone,
   Site settings, Features and Audit log.

SightPress never sends links to sign in or to set a password. It always gives you a code to type on the website
instead. See [Codes we send you](how-to/codes-we-send-you.md).

chunks.heading: Step 9: look at your website
chunks.text:
1. Go to <http://localhost:8080>.
2. You should see the home page, with the heading **Welcome to Riverside Library**, a main menu with About us and
   Contact us, and a footer menu with the privacy notice, the terms of use and the accessibility statement.

Every new website starts with these six pages, already published. Change them in the admin panel under **Pages**.
See [Write and publish a page](how-to/write-and-publish-a-page.md).

The pages follow your computer's light or dark setting, and every page works with a keyboard alone and with a
screen reader. While SightPress runs on your computer, every page asks search engines not to list it.

chunks.heading: Step 10: stop SightPress
chunks.text:
1. Go back to the terminal window where SightPress is running.
2. Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd>. You should see lines that end with `Stopped`.

To start SightPress again later, go to the `skeleton` folder and type `docker compose up` again. Your website and
your account are kept.

chunks.heading: If something goes wrong
chunks.text:
**"port is already allocated" or "address already in use"**
:   Another program on your computer is using one of the ports SightPress needs. See
    [Change the ports SightPress uses](how-to/change-the-ports.md).

**"Cannot connect to the Docker daemon"**
:   Docker is not running. On Windows or macOS, open Docker Desktop and wait until it says that Docker is running.
    On Linux, type `sudo systemctl start docker`.

**The page doesn't load at all**
:   Check that the terminal still shows SightPress running, and that the address is exactly
    `http://localhost:8080`, with `http`, not `https`.

**"APP_SECRET is not set" when you create the site**
:   The secret key is missing from `.env`. Go back to [step 6](#step-6-make-a-settings-file-with-a-secret-key).

**The website shows an error page after you created it**
:   SightPress was not restarted after you added the secret key. Stop it with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> and
    start it again with `docker compose up`.

**"This code doesn't work" on the setup page**
:   Check the e-mail address and the six digits. A setup code works once, for 7 days. To get a new one, see
    [Create a website](how-to/create-a-site.md#give-someone-a-new-setup-code).

chunks.heading: What to do next
chunks.text:
The [how-to guides](how-to/index.md) show you how to write and publish pages, add a language and translate a page,
schedule, move or restore pages, make a site members-only, let people sign up, turn features on or off, search the
website, read its analytics, set up the AI assistant and run SightPress in the background. To move an older
installation to this version, see [Update SightPress](how-to/update-sightpress.md).

To start your website in more than one language, give `site:create` a list in `--locale`, for example
`--locale=en-GB,pt-PT`: every starter page is then written in each language. See
[Add a language and translate a page](how-to/add-a-language.md) to add one later, and
[Turn features on or off](how-to/turn-features-on-or-off.md) to choose the optional features.

You can help improve SightPress without being a developer: see [Report a problem](how-to/report-a-problem.md) and
the other guides under *Help improve SightPress*.

The reference pages explain [roles](reference/roles-and-permissions.md), [blocks](reference/blocks.md),
[search and AI visibility](reference/search-and-ai.md) and the [command line tool](reference/command-line.md).

chunks.page: Add a language and translate a page
chunks.text:
A website can be written in several languages. Each page then has one **translation** per language, with its own
title, address and content. Visitors read the page in their language, and search engines are told which pages are
translations of each other.

You need to be an **admin** to add a language, and an **editor** or **admin** to publish a translation. Contributors
can write translations; an editor publishes them.

chunks.page: Add a language and translate a page
chunks.heading: Add a language
chunks.text:
1. Sign in to the admin panel, for example at <http://localhost:8080/admin>.
2. Choose **Site settings** in the admin menu, then **Change the languages**. You should see the heading
   **Languages** and a table of the languages of the site, the main language first.
3. Under **Add a language**, in **Language to add**, choose the language, for example **Spanish (es)**. You can type
   the first letters of its name to move through the list.
4. Choose **Add language**. You should see the message "Added Spanish. Translate pages into it from each page’s
   editor." and Spanish in the table.

Pages in the **main language** have addresses without a language part, such as `/about`. Pages in the other languages
start with the language code in lower case, such as `/es/about`.

chunks.page: Add a language and translate a page
chunks.heading: Start with the ready-made pages
chunks.text:
New websites come with six starter pages (home, About, Contact, Privacy, Terms and Accessibility). To get them in the
new language too:

1. On the **Languages** screen, choose **Create the starter pages in Spanish**.
2. Each starter page gets a Spanish translation, as a **draft**. Nothing is published until you publish each
   translation (see below).

When SightPress has no ready-made text in that language, the drafts are written in British English for you to
translate, and a message says so.

chunks.page: Add a language and translate a page
chunks.heading: Translate a page
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Pages** in the admin menu, then the page, for example **About us**.
2. In the page editor, go to the **Translations** section. It lists each language of the site with the state of the
   page in it: *Not written yet*, *Draft*, *Draft translation*, *Published*, or *Drafted by the AI assistant, not
   checked yet*.
3. Next to Spanish, choose **Translate into Spanish from British English**. This copies the title, address and
   blocks into a new Spanish draft and opens it. The British English page doesn't change.
4. Translate the title, the address (for example `sobre-nosotros`), the summary and every block, then choose
   **Save page**.

!!! tip "Let the AI assistant draft it"

    If the AI assistant is on, **Draft a translation into Spanish with the AI assistant** writes a first draft for
    you, block by block. It is marked *Drafted by the AI assistant, not checked yet* until a person saves a change or
    chooses **I checked this translation**, and can't be published before that. See
    [Use the AI assistant](use-the-ai-assistant.md).

chunks.page: Add a language and translate a page
chunks.heading: Publish the translation
chunks.text:
1. In the Spanish translation's editor, choose **Publish this translation**. The same checks run as for any page:
   for example, every picture needs a description in Spanish.
2. If a check fails, a list at the top says what to fix. Fix it, save, and publish again.
3. You should see the message "Published the Spanish translation. Visitors can see it now." and **Published** next
   to Spanish in the **Translations** section.

Visitors see a translation only when both the page and the translation are published. A draft translation is not
in the menus, the sitemap or the language links that search engines read.

chunks.page: Add a language and translate a page
chunks.heading: Check it on the website
chunks.text:
1. Go to the page in its new language, for example <http://localhost:8080/es/sobre-nosotros>.
2. You should see the page in Spanish. The menus use the Spanish titles, and the language switcher lists each
   language in its own words, such as "Español".
3. Someone whose browser asks for a language when they open the home page is taken to the home page in that
   language, or the closest one: for example Brazilian Portuguese to European Portuguese, and otherwise the main
   language.

Pictures can have their description, caption and transcript in each language: open the picture in **Media** and
fill in the fields for each language. When a language has none, the main language's text is used, never nothing.

chunks.page: Add a language and translate a page
chunks.heading: Change the main language or remove a language
chunks.text:
- **Make Spanish the main language** changes the addresses of the pages in the old and the new main language. Links
  to their old addresses stop working, so do this early, before the website is public.
- **Remove Spanish** asks you to confirm on its own page. The Spanish translations are **kept** but can't be read.
  Adding Spanish again brings them back. People who chose Spanish for their emails get the main language instead.

chunks.page: Add a language and translate a page
chunks.heading: With the command line tool
chunks.text:
In the `skeleton` folder, replace `demo` with the short name of your website:

```sh
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:locale:add demo es
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:locale:default demo es
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:locale:remove demo es --yes
```

Without `--yes`, `site:locale:remove` only explains what would happen. To start a website in several languages, give
`site:create` a list, such as `--locale=en-GB,pt-PT,es`: every starter page is then written in each of them.

A port is a numbered door on your computer that a program listens on. Each address SightPress uses ends in a port
number, such as the `8080` in `http://localhost:8080`. If another program already uses one of these ports,
SightPress can't start and you see an error such as "port is already allocated". This guide shows you how to
choose different ports.

chunks.heading: The ports SightPress uses
chunks.text:
| Setting              | Default | What it is for                              |
|----------------------|---------|---------------------------------------------|
| `HTTP_PORT`          | 8080    | SightPress itself                           |
| `MAILPIT_UI_PORT`    | 8025    | The test e-mail inbox                       |
| `MAILPIT_SMTP_PORT`  | 1025    | Where the test e-mail inbox receives e-mail |
| `MINIO_API_PORT`     | 9000    | File storage                                |
| `MINIO_CONSOLE_PORT` | 9001    | The file storage console                    |

The error message names the port that is taken, for example `127.0.0.1:8080`.

chunks.heading: Change a port
chunks.text:
1. If SightPress is running, stop it. See [Run SightPress in the background](run-in-the-background.md#stop-sightpress),
   or press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> in the terminal where it runs.
2. In the `skeleton` folder, check whether a file called `.env` exists. If it doesn't, create it by copying the
   example file:

    ```sh
    cp .env.example .env
    ```

    On Windows in PowerShell, `cp` works too.

3. Open `.env` in a text editor, such as Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on macOS. The name starts with a dot, so
   some file browsers hide it; you can open it from the editor's **Open** menu instead.
4. Find the line for the port you want to change, for example `HTTP_PORT=8080`, and change the number, for
   example to `HTTP_PORT=8081`. Pick a number between 1024 and 65535 that no other program uses.
5. Save the file.
6. Start SightPress again with `docker compose up`.
7. Use the new number in the address. With `HTTP_PORT=8081`, go to <http://localhost:8081>. You should see the
   **No site configured** page.

chunks.heading: Who can reach these ports
chunks.text:
Every port listens only on your own computer (the address `127.0.0.1`, also called `localhost`). Other computers on
your network can't reach SightPress.

chunks.page: Change your email address or password
chunks.text: Everyone with an account on a website, members included, can change their own details on **My account**.

chunks.page: Change your email address or password
chunks.heading: Open My account
chunks.text:
Sign in, then choose **My account**: in the admin panel it is a link in the header; on the website, go to `/account`,
for example <http://localhost:8080/account>.

On *My account* you can also change your name, display name, time zone, language (on websites in several languages)
and profile picture. People who use the admin panel can choose **Reduce motion** and **Larger text** there.

chunks.page: Change your email address or password
chunks.heading: Change your password
chunks.text:
1. On *My account*, choose **Change your password**.
2. In **Current password**, type the password you use now.
3. In **New password**, type a new one. The rules are written under the field.
4. Choose **Change password**. You should see "Your password has been changed. You are still signed in here, and
   signed out everywhere else."

If the current password is wrong, a message at the top of the page says so. After five wrong tries in 15 minutes,
you have to wait, as when signing in.

chunks.page: Change your email address or password
chunks.heading: Change your email address
chunks.text:
1. On *My account*, choose **Change your email address**.
2. Type the **New email address** and your **Current password**, then choose **Send the code**.
3. We email a 6-digit code to the **new** address. The email has no link.
4. Type the code on the next page and choose **Confirm my new email address**. You should see "Your email address is
   now …. Sign in with it from now on."

Your old address gets an email saying that the address was changed, with the new one partly hidden and no link.
Until you type the code, nothing changes. See [Codes we send you](codes-we-send-you.md).

Every change is written to the website's audit log, without the passwords.

A SightPress website **never sends you a link** to click. When it needs to check that an e-mail address is yours,
it sends a **6-digit code** instead, and you type that code on the website yourself.

This keeps you safe from fake messages. If you ever get a message that claims to come from a SightPress website and
asks you to click a link, it is not from us. Don't click it.

chunks.heading: When you get a code
chunks.text:
You get a code by e-mail when:

- you **forgot your password** and asked for a new one: the code works for 15 minutes;
- someone **invited you** to help with a website: the invitation code works for 7 days.

The person who sets up a new website gets a **setup code** from the command line tool, not by e-mail. They pass it
on to the website's first admin, who uses it to choose a password. A setup code works for 7 days.

Each code works only once.

chunks.heading: What a code message looks like
chunks.text:
- The subject names the website, for example "Your code to reset your password for Riverside Library" or "Ada
  invited you to Riverside Library". The code itself is never in the subject.
- The message has the code on its own line, for example `123 456`.
- The message has no links, no web addresses and no pictures.
- It ends with: "We will never send you a link. Type this code on the page where you asked for it. Never share it
  with anyone."

chunks.heading: Type a code
chunks.text:
1. Go to the page that asked for the code. For a password, that is the page you are already on. For an invitation,
   go to the website's sign-in page and choose **Accept an invitation**.
2. Find the field called **6-digit code**.
3. Type the 6 digits. You can type them with or without the space in the middle.
4. Choose **Continue**. The page never sends the code by itself, so take your time.
5. You should see the next step, for example a page where you choose your password.

chunks.heading: If the code doesn't work
chunks.text:
- Check the digits and try again. After 5 wrong tries the code stops working.
- A code also stops working when it is too old, when it has been used, or when you asked for a newer one.
- On the password page, choose **Send a new code**. You can ask for a new code once a minute; if it is too soon,
  the page tells you how many seconds to wait.
- For an invitation, ask the person who invited you to invite you again.
- For a setup code, ask the person who set up the website for a new one.

chunks.heading: Try it on your computer
chunks.text:
When SightPress runs on your computer, the e-mails with codes go to the test inbox. See
[Open the test e-mail inbox](open-the-test-email-inbox.md).

One SightPress installation can run many websites. Each website has its own pages, people, files and settings,
kept in its own database. This guide shows you how to create a website with the command line tool, and what each
part of the command means.

Before you start, follow [Getting started](../getting-started.md) up to step 6, so that SightPress runs and has a
secret key.

chunks.heading: Create the website, answering questions
chunks.text:
The easiest way is to let the command ask you everything, one question at a time.

1. Open a terminal and go to the `skeleton` folder.
2. Type:

    ```sh
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create
    ```

3. Answer each question and press Enter. Each question says what to type. When it ends with "Press Enter for"
   and a value, pressing Enter without typing takes that value. When it lists choices, such as "Type person or
   organization", type one of them; capital letters don't matter.
4. For the database, the command first asks which engine to use. Press Enter for **SQLite**: it keeps the
   website in one file and needs nothing else. Press Enter again to keep the file in the `sites` folder. If you
   choose MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL instead, the command asks for the server, port, database name, user name and
   password one by one, each with a usual value you can keep with Enter. The password isn't shown as you type it,
   and you type it twice so a typing mistake is caught.
5. For the main language, type a code such as `en-GB` or `pt-BR`. Capital letters don't matter and you can use
   `_` instead of `-`. The command says the language in words, for example "That is Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR).
   Is that right?". Type `yes` or press Enter if it is, or `no` to type it again.
6. If an answer isn't right, for example an e-mail address without the part after `@`, the command says what is
   wrong and asks again. After 3 wrong answers in a row i

chunks.heading: Create the website with one command
chunks.text:
If you already know every answer, for example in a script, give them all on one line. The command then asks
nothing. This example creates a website called "Riverside Library" for an organisation:

```sh
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create demo --domain=localhost --db-engine=sqlite --url=http://localhost:8080 --owner-type=organization --locale=en-GB --name="Riverside Library" --admin-email=ada@example.org --admin-first-name=Ada --admin-last-name=Lovelace
```

If something is wrong, the command says what, and creates nothing.

chunks.heading: What each part means
chunks.text:
| Part | What to give | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `demo` | A short name for the website: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. You use it in other commands. | `library` |
| `--domain` | The web addresses of the website, without `https://`, separated by commas. Each address belongs to one website only. On your own computer, use `localhost`. | `library.example.org,www.library.example.org` |
| `--db-engine` | The database engine: `sqlite`, `mysql`, `mariadb` or `postgresql`. On your own computer, SQLite is simplest. See [Start a database server](start-a-database.md) for the others. | `sqlite` |
| `--db-path` | For SQLite: the file. Optional: without it, a file named after the short name in the `sites` folder. | `library.sqlite` |
| `--db-host`, `--db-port`, `--db-name`, `--db-user`, `--db-password` | For the other engines: the server, its port, the database, and the user name and password. Without them, `localhost`, the engine's usual port, `sightpress_` and the short name, `sightpress` and no password. | `--db-host=db --db-user=library` |
| `--db` | Instead of the parts above: the whole database address in one go. | `sqlite:////app/sites/library.sqlite` |
| `--owner-type` | Who runs the website: `organization` or `person`, in capitals or not. The ready-made pages say "we" for an organisation and "I" for a person. | `person` |
| `--locale` | The website's main language. Capital letters don't matter, and `_` works as well as `-`. | `en-GB`, `pt_br`, `fr-FR` |
| `--name` |

chunks.heading: What a new website has
Try SightPress with demo content
chunks.text:
Add `--with-demo-content` to the command to fill the new website with examples:

- five files in the media library: a picture, a short video with captions, a sound recording and a PDF;
- a page called "Every kind of block" at `/every-block`, with one block of every kind, and a page under it;
- three more people, each waiting for their setup code: Bea Okafor (editor), Cleo Martins (contributor) and Max
  Müller (member).

The command prints a setup code for each person. The `example.org` addresses can't receive e-mail, so give the codes
to whoever tries the website out.

chunks.heading: Give someone a new setup code
chunks.text:
A setup code works once, for 7 days. To make a new one for an admin who hasn't chosen a password yet, type:

```sh
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:user:create-admin demo --email=ada@example.org --first-name=Ada --last-name=Lovelace --url=http://localhost:8080
```

You should see a new setup code. The old one stops working. The same command adds another admin when you give a new
e-mail address. Someone who already has a password uses **Forgot your password?** on the sign-in page instead.

chunks.heading: Turn a website off, or remove it
chunks.text:
| To | Type | Visitors see |
| --- | --- | --- |
| turn it off for a while | `bin/sightpress site:disable demo` | "temporarily unavailable" |
| turn it on again | `bin/sightpress site:enable demo` | the website |
| close it and keep its data | `bin/sightpress site:archive demo` | "gone" |
| delete it, softly | `bin/sightpress site:delete demo` | "not found"; the data is kept |
| remove a deleted website for good | `bin/sightpress site:purge demo` | — |

Start each command with `docker compose run --rm --no-deps php`, as above. `site:purge` keeps the database unless
you add `--drop-database`, which can't be undone. The [command line reference](../reference/command-line.md) lists
every command.

How large a file you can upload depends on two things: what the website accepts for each kind of file, and what the
server accepts in one go. This guide explains the warning admins see when the server's settings are too low, and
how to change them.

chunks.heading: What you see
chunks.text:
- Next to the upload field in **Media**, everyone sees the largest file they can upload, for example "Largest file
  you can upload: pictures 20 MB, documents 50 MB, audio files 64 MB and videos 64 MB."
- If you choose a file that is too large, the browser refuses it before sending it. The reason appears under the
  field, which gets focus, so screen readers read it out.
- If something too large is sent anyway, you see a page called **This is too large to send**. It says how much the
  server accepts and has a **Go back to the form** link.
- Admins see a warning called **Your server’s settings stop some uploads** on the dashboard and in **Media**. Each
  point names a server setting and the value it needs. Editors and contributors don't see it.

chunks.heading: Change the limits on your own computer
chunks.text:
With SightPress running in Docker, the limits are one group of lines in the `.env` file of the `skeleton` folder.
PHP and the web server both read them, so they always match.

1. If there is no `.env` file in the `skeleton` folder yet, create it by copying the example:

    ```sh
    cp .env.example .env
    ```

2. Open `.env` in a text editor and find the lines that start with `UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE`.
3. Change the values you need:

    | Setting            | Recommended | What it is                                                      |
    |--------------------|-------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
    | `UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE`  | `64M`       | The largest file in one upload                                  |
    | `INPUT_MAX_SIZE`   | `8M`        | The largest form without files, such as a long page             |
    | `INPUT_MAX_VARS`   | `5000`      | How many fields one form can have; lower values can lose content |
    | `MAX_FILE_UPLOADS` | `20`        | How many files one upload can hold                               |
    | `PHP_MEMORY_LIMIT` | `256M`      | Memory for one request; `512M` for pictures over 25 million pixels |
    | `UPLOAD_TIMEOUT`   | `300`       | Seconds a slow upload may take                                   |

    Sizes are whole megabytes or gigabytes, such as `64M` or `1G`. On a small site or shared hosting, `32M` is
    enough for `UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE`.

4. Save the file and restart SightPress:

chunks.heading: On a hosting provider's server
chunks.text:
If someone else runs your server, send them the warning's text. It names the settings, for example
`upload_max_filesize`, `post_max_size` or the web server's limit (`client_max_body_size` for nginx), and the value
each needs. Ask them to tell you when it is done, then open the dashboard again: the warning is gone once the
settings are right.

chunks.heading: Large audio files and videos
chunks.text:
The website accepts audio files up to 200 MB and videos up to 1 GB, but for now one upload can't be larger than
`UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE`. A later version will send large files in parts, so they can be larger than the server's limit.
`system:check` mentions this as a note, not a problem.

By default only people you invite can have an account on your website. You can also let anyone create their own
account. They confirm their email address with a 6-digit code before they can sign in.

You need to be an **admin**.

chunks.heading: Turn sign-up on
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Site settings** in the admin menu, then **Change who can sign up**.
2. Tick **Let anyone create an account**.
3. In **Role of people who sign up**, keep **Member** unless you have a reason to change it. Members can read
   members-only pages and nothing more. Only roles that are safe to give to people you don't know are listed: never
   editor or admin.
4. Choose **Save sign-up settings**. You should see "The sign-up settings have been saved."

The sign-in page now shows "New here?" with a **Create an account** link.

chunks.heading: Try it as a new person
chunks.text:
1. Sign out, or open a private browser window, and go to the sign-in page, for example
   <http://localhost:8080/login>.
2. Choose **Create an account**. Fill in your first name, last name, an optional display name, your email address,
   your time zone (your browser's is already chosen) and a password. On a website in several languages, choose your
   language too.
3. Choose **Create my account**. You should see the heading **Confirm your email address**.
4. Open the email. While you try SightPress on your computer, it is in the test inbox: see
   [Open the test e-mail inbox](open-the-test-email-inbox.md). It has a 6-digit code and **no link**.
5. Type the code in **6-digit code** and choose **Confirm my email address**. You should see "Your email address is
   confirmed and your account is ready."
6. Sign in with your email address and password.

The code works once, for 15 minutes. **Send a new code** sends another one, at most once a minute. See
[Codes we send you](codes-we-send-you.md).

chunks.heading: What keeps it safe
chunks.text:
- An account can't sign in until its email address is confirmed. Accounts that are never confirmed are removed after
  a week.
- If someone signs up with an address that already has an account, the page looks exactly the same, so nobody can find
  out who has an account. The owner of the address gets an email saying someone tried, with no link.
- A hidden field catches most automated sign-ups, and each place can send at most 10 sign-up forms an hour. There are
  no picture puzzles.
- Every new account and every change to these settings is written to the **Audit log**.

To turn sign-up off again, untick **Let anyone create an account**. Accounts that were already made are kept.

chunks.page: Make a website or a page members-only
chunks.text:
A **members-only** page can only be read by people who have an account on the website and are signed in. You can
make a single page members-only, or the whole website.

You need to be an **admin** to change the whole website, and an **editor** or **admin** to change a page.

chunks.page: Make a website or a page members-only
chunks.heading: Make one page members-only
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Pages** in the admin menu, then the page.
2. In **About the page**, under **Who can read this page**, choose **Members only: people with an account on the
   site, once they sign in**.
3. Choose **Save page**.
4. Check: sign out, or open a private browser window, and go to the page. You should see the sign-in page. After
   signing in, you are taken back to the page.

A members-only page is left out of search engines, the sitemap, `llms.txt` and site search for visitors who aren't
signed in. In the menus, it only appears for people who are signed in.

To show a menu entry only to members, for example a link to a members' forum, choose **Menus**, then **Change** next
to the entry, and tick **Only show this entry to members who are signed in**.

chunks.page: Make a website or a page members-only
chunks.heading: Make the whole website members-only
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Site settings** in the admin menu.
2. Under **Who can read the site**, choose **Only people with an account, once they sign in. Search engines and AI
   services can’t read any page.**
3. Choose **Save settings**. You should see "The settings have been saved."
4. Check: in a private browser window, go to any page of the website. You should see the sign-in page with the
   message "This site is for its members. Sign in to read it."

On a members-only website:

- People who aren't signed in can still sign in, create an account (if you let them, see
  [Let people sign up](let-people-sign-up.md)), reset a forgotten password and accept an invitation.
- Search engines and AI services can't read anything: the sitemap and `llms.txt` are empty, and every page asks not
  to be listed.
- Every signed-in person, whatever their role, can read every published page.

chunks.page: Make a website or a page members-only
chunks.heading: Who can read what
chunks.text:
| | Visitors who aren't signed in | Members (signed in) | Editors and admins |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pages for everyone, on a public website | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Members-only pages | No: asked to sign in | Yes | Yes |
| Any page of a members-only website | No: asked to sign in | Yes | Yes |
| Drafts, older versions, archived pages | No | No | Yes |
| The admin panel | No | No | Yes |

To give people accounts, invite them from **Invite someone** in the admin menu, or let them sign up themselves.

chunks.page: Move or rename a page without breaking links
chunks.text:
When a published page gets a new address, or moves somewhere else on the website, SightPress remembers its old
address. Anyone who follows an old link or bookmark is taken to the new address, and search engines are told that the
page has moved for good. You don't need to do anything for this to happen.

You need to be an **editor** or **admin**.

chunks.page: Move or rename a page without breaking links
chunks.heading: Give a page a new address
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Pages** in the admin menu, then the page.
2. In **Address**, type the new last part of the address, for example `opening-times` instead of `hours`. Use
   lower-case letters, digits and hyphens.
3. Choose **Save page**.
4. Check: open the old address, for example <http://localhost:8080/hours>. You should land on
   <http://localhost:8080/opening-times>.

Pages under it move with it: `/hours/holidays` becomes `/opening-times/holidays`, and its old address leads there
too.

chunks.page: Move or rename a page without breaking links
chunks.heading: Move a page somewhere else on the website
chunks.text:
In the page editor, the **Place in the site** section has these buttons:

- **Move up** and **Move down** change the order of pages at the same level, for example in a menu of pages.
- **Move under the page before it** puts the page one level down, under the page just above it.
- **Move out to the level above** puts the page one level up.
- **Move to**: choose **The top level of the site** or any other page in the list, then choose **Move the page**.

After each move, a message says where the page is now, and focus stays in the section. Pages under it move with it,
and every old address leads to the new one.

chunks.page: Move or rename a page without breaking links
chunks.heading: See and change the redirects
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Redirects** in the admin menu. You should see the table **Old addresses and where they lead**, with each
   **Old address**, its **Language** and where it **Leads to**. A page that was deleted for good shows "Gone: the
   page was deleted".
2. To stop an old address leading anywhere, choose **Remove the redirect from** followed by that address.
3. To add your own, for example for a page from an old website, fill in **Old address** (such as `/old-news`) and
   **New address** (such as `/news`) under **Add a redirect**, then choose **Add redirect**. The new address must be
   in the same language.

A few rules keep this tidy:

- If a page moves twice, its oldest address leads straight to the newest one, never through a chain.
- A redirect that would go round in a circle is refused.
- A new page that uses an old address wins: the redirect stops and visitors see the new page.

The **Pages not found** report on the *Analytics* screen lists addresses people asked for that don't exist, with a
link to add a redirect for each. See [See who visits your website](see-who-visits-your-website.md).

SightPress comes with a file storage program called MinIO, which has its own web console. This guide shows you how
to sign in to it.

1. Start SightPress (see [Getting started](../getting-started.md)).
2. In your web browser, go to <http://localhost:9001>.
3. You should see the MinIO sign-in page.
4. Sign in with the user name `sightpress` and the password `sightpress-secret`.
5. You should see the MinIO console. There are no files yet.

In this version, websites don't use MinIO yet. Each website keeps its uploaded files, such as pictures and documents,
in its own folder inside the `sites` folder of the `skeleton`. A later version will let websites store their files in
MinIO or another storage service.

If you changed `MINIO_ROOT_USER`, `MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` or `MINIO_CONSOLE_PORT` in your `.env` file, use your
values instead. These settings only take effect the first time the storage starts.

When SightPress runs on your computer, it never sends real e-mail. Every message goes to a test inbox called
Mailpit instead, so you can read it without anything leaving your computer. This guide shows you how to open it.

1. Start SightPress (see [Getting started](../getting-started.md)).
2. In your web browser, go to <http://localhost:8025>.
3. You should see the Mailpit inbox. It is empty for now, with a message saying there are no messages.

SightPress sends e-mail when:

- someone forgets their password and asks for a code;
- someone is invited to help with a website;
- a page is sent for review: every editor and admin is told;
- a visitor sends a message with a contact form.

Each of these messages appears here a moment later. Choose a message to read it.

The inbox only gets messages when your `.env` file has the line `MAILER_DSN=smtp://mailpit:1025`. The file you copied
from `.env.example` in [Getting started](../getting-started.md) already has it. Without it, SightPress sends nothing.

If you changed `MAILPIT_UI_PORT` in your `.env` file, use that number instead of `8025`.

chunks.page: Put a page in the trash and get it back
chunks.text:
You can take a page off the website in two ways, and both keep it so you can bring it back:

- **Archive** keeps the page out of sight. Visitors who open its address are told the page isn't found.
- **Put in the trash** is for pages you want to get rid of. Visitors who open its address are told the page is
  **gone**, so search engines drop it. A page stays in the trash until someone deletes it for good.

You need to be an **editor** or **admin**.

chunks.page: Put a page in the trash and get it back
chunks.heading: Archive a page
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Pages** in the admin menu, then the page.
2. Choose **Archive**. You should see "Archived. Visitors can’t see the page any more; it is kept with the archived
   pages."
3. To bring it back, open it again and choose **Restore as a draft**. It comes back as a draft: publish it again when
   it is ready.

chunks.page: Put a page in the trash and get it back
chunks.heading: Put a page in the trash
chunks.text:
1. Open the page in the editor.
2. Choose **Put in the trash**. You should see "Put in the trash. Its address now tells visitors the page is gone."

A page with pages under it can only go in the trash once those pages are in the trash already, so nothing is left
without a page above it.

chunks.page: Put a page in the trash and get it back
chunks.heading: Find a page in the trash and get it back
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Pages** in the admin menu.
2. In the **State** filter, choose **In the trash**, then choose **Show pages**. You should see only the pages in the trash.
3. Open the page and choose **Take out of the trash**. You should see "Restored as a draft. Publish it again when it
   is ready."

A page comes out of the trash as a draft, and only when the page above it isn't in the trash.

chunks.page: Put a page in the trash and get it back
chunks.heading: Delete a page for good
chunks.text:
This can't be undone.

1. Open a page that is in the trash.
2. Choose **Delete this page for good**. A page asks you to confirm, and lists what goes with it: the pages under it,
   every translation and every older version.
3. Choose **Delete for good** to go ahead, or **Keep it in the trash** to go back.

Its address then tells visitors and search engines that the page is gone, until a new page uses the address. Menu
entries that pointed to it are removed.

chunks.page: Put a page in the trash and get it back
chunks.heading: Copy a page
chunks.text:
**Copy this page** makes a new draft right after the page, in every language it is written in, titled "Copy of …",
with `-copy` added to its address. The pages under it aren't copied. The copy opens in the editor.

Every step on this page is written to the website’s audit log, which admins can read.

If something in SightPress doesn't work, shows an error, or stops you from doing something with your keyboard,
screen reader, zoom or colour settings, please tell us. You don't need to know which part of SightPress is at fault.

chunks.heading: What to tell us
chunks.text:
Whichever way you report it, these help us most:

1. What you were trying to do, for example "publish a page in Spanish".
2. What happened. Copy any error message as text.
3. What you expected to happen.
4. The SightPress version, if you know it, and your browser and operating system.
5. For an **accessibility barrier**: your assistive technology and its version, if you use one, and what was
   announced or what happened.

Accessibility barriers are always treated as bugs, never as feature requests.

chunks.heading: Report it by email (no GitHub account needed)
chunks.text:
1. Write an email to <contribute@sightpress.org>, in any format that suits you: text, a voice recording or a
   document. Write in your own words; imperfect English is welcome.
2. A maintainer replies within 5 working days, adds the report to GitHub for you, and tells you what happens next.

chunks.heading: Report it on GitHub
chunks.text:
If you have a GitHub account:

1. Go to [open an issue in SightPress core](https://github.com/sightpress/core/issues/new/choose). If the problem is
   in this documentation, use [the docs issues](https://github.com/sightpress/docs/issues/new/choose) instead; if you
   aren't sure, use core and we'll move it.
2. Choose **Report a problem**, or **Report an accessibility barrier**. Each form says which fields are required, in
   words.
3. Fill in the form and choose **Submit new issue**.

A maintainer replies, asks for anything that is missing and labels the issue.

chunks.heading: Security problems
chunks.text:
Never report a security problem in public. Email <security@sightpress.org>, or use **Report a vulnerability** on the
*Security* tab of the repository on GitHub. We acknowledge every report within 5 working days.

chunks.heading: Problems with people
chunks.text:
To report behaviour that breaks the
[Code of Conduct](https://github.com/sightpress/docs/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), email
<conduct@sightpress.org>. Reports are confidential.

chunks.page: Restore an older version of a page
chunks.text:
Every time a page is saved, SightPress keeps a version of it. You can see who saved each version and when, read what
changed, word by word, and bring an older version back. Restoring never publishes anything.

You need to be able to change the page: a **contributor** for your own drafts, or an **editor** or **admin**.

chunks.page: Restore an older version of a page
chunks.heading: See the older versions
chunks.text:
1. Choose **Pages** in the admin menu, then the page.
2. Next to the page's state, choose **Older versions**. You should see a table of versions, newest first: the
   version number, when it was saved (in your own time zone), who saved it, and the state the page was in then.
   "The system" means a change made from the command line or on a schedule.

On a website in several languages, each translation has its own versions. Links at the top of the screen lead to the
versions in each language.

chunks.page: Restore an older version of a page
chunks.heading: See what changed
chunks.text:
1. Choose a version number, for example **Version 3**. You should see what changed since the version before it: first
   the details of the page (title, address, summary, search fields), then each block, under a heading that says
   whether it was changed, added, removed or has no changes.
2. Inside a field, words that were taken out read "[removed: …]" and are crossed out; words that were put in read
   "[added: …]" and are underlined.

The words "removed" and "added" are always written out, so the comparison reads the same with a screen reader, in
high contrast mode and without colours.

chunks.page: Restore an older version of a page
chunks.heading: Bring a version back
chunks.text:
1. On the version's screen, choose **Restore version 3** (with that version's number).
2. You should see "Restored version 3 as version 5. Nothing was published: the page is still a draft." The newer
   versions stay in the list, so you can change your mind.

Restoring brings back the title, address, search fields and blocks. It doesn't change the layout, who can read the
page or its place on the website.

**While the page is published, restoring is refused**, because visitors would see the old text straight away. Choose
**Unpublish** first (or make that translation a draft), restore the version, check it, and publish again.

A version with a block that no longer exists can't be restored: copy what you need from it instead.

SightPress is led by blind people. Sighted reviewers help us check what is hard to check without sight. You don't
need to know anything about design or code: if something looks wrong to you, it probably is.

chunks.heading: What to check
chunks.text:
Go through a few screens of the admin panel and of a website (see [Getting started](../getting-started.md) to run
your own) and look for these:

1. **Contrast.** Is any text, icon or border hard to see? Check in light mode, in dark mode, and with a high
   contrast theme (on Windows, *Settings → Accessibility → Contrast themes*).
2. **Focus.** Press <kbd>Tab</kbd> again and again. Can you always see where you are?
3. **Zoom.** Zoom the browser to 200% and to 400% (<kbd>Ctrl</kbd> and <kbd>+</kbd>, or <kbd>Cmd</kbd> and
   <kbd>+</kbd> on a Mac). Is any text cut off or on top of other text? Do you have to scroll sideways to read a line?
4. **Small screens.** Make the window very narrow, about the width of a small phone. Does everything still fit?
5. **Spacing.** Is anything squashed together or badly lined up?
6. **Pictures.** Do the icons, the generated profile pictures, the sharing images and the charts look right? Are
   the screenshots in the documentation up to date?
7. **Labels.** Does the text you see on a button or a field match what it does? A screen reader announces the same
   words, so they must make sense on their own.
8. **Colour alone.** Is any information shown only by colour, such as red for an error, without words?

chunks.heading: How to describe a screenshot
Send your review
chunks.text:
On GitHub, [open an issue](https://github.com/sightpress/core/issues/new/choose) and choose **Interface review**.
The form asks for the screen, your browser, zoom level and colour mode, what looks wrong, and a description of any
screenshot. Without a GitHub account, email the same to <contribute@sightpress.org>.

In [Getting started](../getting-started.md), SightPress runs in a terminal window and stops when you close it.
This guide shows you how to run it in the background instead.

chunks.heading: Start SightPress
chunks.text:
1. Open a terminal and go to the `skeleton` folder, for example:

    ```sh
    cd sightpress/skeleton
    ```

2. Type:

    ```sh
    docker compose up --detach --wait
    ```

3. Wait until the command finishes. You should see one line per container (`php`, `nginx`, `mailpit` and
   `minio`), each ending with `Healthy`. You get your terminal back.
4. Go to <http://localhost:8080>. You should see the **No site configured** page.

    The very first time, SightPress keeps installing for a minute or two after the command finishes, and the
    browser shows **502 Bad Gateway**. Wait a minute, then reload the page.

You can now close the terminal. SightPress keeps running until you stop it or restart your computer.

chunks.heading: See what is running
chunks.text:
Type:

```sh
docker compose ps
```

You should see a table with one row for each container. The **STATUS** column says `Up` and how long the
container has been running.

chunks.heading: Read the messages SightPress writes
chunks.text:
Type:

```sh
docker compose logs --follow
```

You see the messages from every container, and new ones as they arrive. Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to
stop reading. SightPress keeps running.

chunks.heading: Stop SightPress
chunks.text:
Type:

```sh
docker compose --profile "*" down
```

You should see lines ending with `Removed`. The `--profile "*"` part also stops a database server if you started
one. Your settings and stored files are kept for next time.

!!! tip "Shortcuts for macOS and Linux"

    If the `make` program is installed, you can type `make up` to start SightPress in the background and
    `make down` to stop it. Type `make` on its own to list every shortcut.

A page can be published at a set time, and taken off the website again at another time, without anyone being there
to press a button. This is useful for an event page that should appear on Monday morning, or a notice that should
disappear when an offer ends.

You need to be an **editor** or **admin**: people who may publish pages.

chunks.heading: Before you start
chunks.text:
SightPress does what is scheduled once a minute, with a helper called the **scheduler**. When you start SightPress
with `docker compose up` (see [Getting started](../getting-started.md)), the scheduler starts too. To see what it
does, type `docker compose logs -f scheduler` in the `skeleton` folder.

chunks.heading: Publish a page at a set time
chunks.text:
1. Write the page and take it through review until it is **Approved** (see
   [Write and publish a page](write-and-publish-a-page.md)). Only an approved page can be published on schedule.
2. In the page editor, go to the **Schedule** section. It says "Nothing is scheduled." and shows **your time zone**
   above the fields. Change your time zone on *My account* if it is wrong.
3. In **Publish at**, choose the day and time.
4. Choose **Save the schedule**. You should see a message such as "Scheduled: the page is published at 1 Dec 2026,
   09:00 (Europe/London time)."
5. In the page list, the page shows "Approved · To be published at 1 Dec 2026, 09:00".

Within a minute of that time, the page is published.

chunks.heading: Take a page off the website at a set time
chunks.text:
1. In the **Schedule** section, choose a time in **Take off the site at**.
2. Choose **Save the schedule**.

At that time the page becomes a draft again, if it is published then.

chunks.heading: Change or clear the schedule
chunks.text:
Change the times and choose **Save the schedule** again, or choose **Clear the schedule** to remove both times.
Archiving a page or putting it in the trash clears its schedule too.

chunks.heading: If something goes wrong
chunks.text:
- **A time in the past**, an end before the start, or a time that doesn't exist (the night the clocks go forward) is
  explained, and the form keeps what you typed.
- The page is published **as the person who scheduled it**: the same publish checks run. If a check fails, or that
  person may no longer publish, nothing is published, the audit log says why, and the time is cleared so that
  you can fix the page and schedule it again.
- If the computer or server was off at the time, the page is published as soon as the scheduler runs again.

Whoever runs SightPress on a server sets the scheduler up once; see the [command line reference](../reference/command-line.md#things-that-happen-at-a-set-time).

Every page of a website has a search box in its header. It finds the website's published pages in the language you
are reading, by their title, their summary and their text, including the descriptions of pictures, the transcripts
of recordings and the names of downloads. Site search is an optional feature, on by default.

chunks.heading: Search from any page
chunks.text:
1. Open any page of your website, for example `http://localhost:8080/`.
2. In the header, find **Search this site**. With a keyboard, press Tab until you reach the search box.
3. Type one or more words, for example `opening hours`, and press Enter (or choose **Search**).
4. You should see the results page. Its title and heading say what you searched for and how many results there are,
   for example "2 results for “opening hours”". Screen readers read this out when the page opens.
5. Each result has its title as a link, where it is on the website ("In: About us › Team") and a few lines of its
   text with the words you searched for in bold and underlined. Choose a title to open the page.

Good to know:

- Capitals and accents don't matter: `cafe` finds "Café".
- Words are matched by their stem: `libraries` finds "library".
- The last word can be the start of a word: `accessib` finds "accessibility".
- Pages with every word come first. When no page has every word, the results page says so and shows pages with some
  of them.
- With ten results or more, links at the bottom ("Search results pages") lead to the next pages.

chunks.heading: When nothing is found
chunks.text:
The page says "No results for …" and gives tips: check the spelling, try fewer or other words. On a website in
several languages, the language list at the top leads to the same search in the other languages.

chunks.heading: Pages for members only
chunks.text:
Pages for members only are found only by people who are signed in. Sign in, search again, and they appear in the
results.

chunks.heading: Leave a page out of the search
chunks.text:
1. Open the page in the admin panel's page editor.
2. In the **Search & AI** section, tick **Leave this page out of the site’s own search**.
3. Choose **Save**.
4. Check: searching for the page's title no longer finds it. Search engines can still list the page, unless you also
   tick **Ask search engines and AI search engines not to list this page**.

The choice is made for each language of the page.

chunks.heading: If new pages don't show up
chunks.text:
The search follows every change as it is saved. After a bigger change (adding a language, changing the website's
main language, making the whole website members-only, or turning search back on), SightPress rebuilds the search
within a minute, as long as it runs in the background (see
[Run SightPress in the background](run-in-the-background.md)). To rebuild it straight away, in the `skeleton` folder
type (replace `demo` with your website's short name):

```sh
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:search:reindex demo
```

You should see one line per language, such as `en-GB: 12 documents indexed.`

chunks.heading: Turn search off
chunks.text:
Search is a feature: an admin can turn it off on the **Features** screen (see
[Turn features on or off](turn-features-on-or-off.md)). The search box and the results page are then gone.

SightPress counts how many people visit your website, which pages they read, where they come from, what they search
for and which addresses are not found. It also shows which search engines and AI crawlers read the website.
Analytics is an optional feature, on by default.

It is private by design: visits are counted on your own server, with no cookies, no tracking scripts and nothing
sent to other companies. SightPress never stores visitors' IP addresses or details of their browser. This is not
legal advice, but it means most websites don't need a cookie banner for it.

chunks.heading: Open the Analytics screen
chunks.text:
1. Sign in to the admin panel as an admin or an editor, for example at `http://localhost:8080/admin`.
2. In the admin menu, choose **Analytics**. (Contributors don't have it.)
3. You should see the last 30 days. Under **Days to show**, the link for the range you are looking at is marked as
   the current one; choose **Last 7 days**, **Last 90 days** or **Last 12 months** to change it.
4. For other dates, fill in **First day** and **Last day** under **Other days** and choose **Show these days**. If a
   date is missing or the last day comes before the first, a box at the top says "There is a problem" and links to
   the field to fix.

Days run from midnight to midnight in your website's time zone, which the screen names, so everyone sees the same
numbers. Today's numbers are counted live.

chunks.heading: Read the numbers
chunks.text:
At the top, three sentences sum up the range, for example "1,349 visitors, up 12% on the 30 days before". The arrows
next to them are only decoration: the words say the same.

Each part of the screen has its own heading, so a screen reader can move between them:

- **Visitors over time**: a chart, with a sentence above it that says what it shows, for example "Visitors went up
  12% compared with the previous 30 days, from 1,204 to 1,349. The busiest day was Tuesday 4 November, with 98
  visitors." This period is a solid line with round markers, the period before a dashed line with square markers.
  Choose **Show the data for each day** to see every day in a table.
- **Pages read most**, **Where visitors came from** and **Devices** (phone, tablet or computer): tables, with a
  small bar next to each number.
- **Languages**: only on websites in more than one language.
- **Site search**: what people searched for, and the searches that found nothing. Only while site search is on.
  Searches that look like an email address or a phone number are counted but never shown.
- **Pages not found**: addresses people asked for that don't exist. People who can edit any page see **Add a
  redirect** next to each one: it opens the Redirects screen with the address filled in.
- **Search engines and AI crawlers**: which programs read the website and what they read. They are never counted
  as visitors.

Each part has a **Download … as a CSV file** link, for a spreadsheet. The file has every row

chunks.heading: What is counted and what isn't
chunks.text:
- A visitor is counted once per day. The same person on two days counts twice; there is no "returning visitors"
  number, on purpose.
- Not counted: people signed in to the website, visitors whose browser asks websites not to track them (Global
  Privacy Control or Do Not Track), the admin panel, pictures and other files, and pages a browser only loads in
  advance.
- Figures are kept for 25 months, so you can compare two full years.

chunks.heading: The dashboard
chunks.text:
The dashboard (`/admin`) shows **Last 7 days**: one sentence with the visitors and page views of the last week, and
a link to the Analytics screen.

chunks.heading: Keep analytics for less time, or delete them (admins)
chunks.text:
1. On the Analytics screen, go to **Keeping analytics** at the bottom.
2. In **Months to keep analytics for**, type a number from 1 to 25 and choose **Save**. Older figures are deleted
   within the hour. The change is in the audit log.
3. To delete everything, choose **Delete analytics data**. A page asks you to confirm; choose **Delete analytics
   data** again, or **Keep the data** to go back. Counting goes on from then.

chunks.heading: From the command line
chunks.text:
In the `skeleton` folder (replace `demo` with your website's short name):

```sh
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:analytics:report demo
```

You should see the visitors, page views and views per visitor of the last 30 days, each with the 30 days before.
Add `--report=pages` (or `sources`, `devices`, `not-found` …) for another report, and `--format=csv` or
`--format=json` for a file. If it warns that analytics were "last rolled up" long ago, SightPress isn't running in
the background (see [Run SightPress in the background](run-in-the-background.md)).

chunks.heading: Turn analytics off
chunks.text:
Analytics is a feature: an admin can turn it off on the **Features** screen (see
[Turn features on or off](turn-features-on-or-off.md)). Nothing is counted any more, and the figures already
counted are kept until they are deleted. If your website's **Privacy notice** page was written by SightPress, remove
its "Visitor statistics" section.

SightPress keeps its data in a single file on disk (an SQLite database), so it doesn't need a separate database
server. If you want to try one, SightPress can start MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL for you. This guide shows you how.

!!! note "Not used yet"

    At this stage SightPress starts the database server but doesn't store anything in it. You can check that it
    runs. Later versions will let you use it for your sites.

chunks.heading: Start SightPress with a database
chunks.text:
1. If SightPress is running, stop it with `docker compose --profile "*" down`.
2. In the `skeleton` folder, type one of these commands:

    ```sh
    docker compose --profile mysql up
    ```

    For MariaDB, use `--profile mariadb`. For PostgreSQL, use `--profile postgres`.

3. Wait until the text stops scrolling. The first time, Docker downloads the database, which can take a few minutes.
   You should see lines starting with `mysql-1` (or `mariadb-1`, or `postgres-1`) among the others.

To start it in the background instead, add `--detach --wait` to the end of the command.

chunks.heading: Check that the database runs
chunks.text:
1. Open a second terminal and go to the `skeleton` folder.
2. Type:

    ```sh
    docker compose --profile "*" ps
    ```

3. You should see a row for the database, such as `mysql`, with `(healthy)` in the **STATUS** column. If it says
   `(health: starting)`, wait a few seconds and type the command again.

When you start SightPress without `--profile`, no database server runs, and this table has no database row.

chunks.heading: The database settings
chunks.text:
The database is created with these values. You can change them in the `.env` file before the first start (see
[Change the ports SightPress uses](change-the-ports.md#change-a-port) for how to create and edit `.env`).

| Setting            | Default           | What it is                                  |
|--------------------|-------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| `DB_NAME`          | `sightpress`      | The name of the database                    |
| `DB_USER`          | `sightpress`      | The user name                               |
| `DB_PASSWORD`      | `sightpress`      | The user's password                         |
| `DB_ROOT_PASSWORD` | `sightpress-root` | The administrator password (MySQL, MariaDB) |

The database server can only be reached by the other SightPress containers, not from your computer or your network.

chunks.heading: Stop the database
chunks.text:
Type `docker compose --profile "*" down`. This stops SightPress and the database. The data in the database is kept
for next time.

If you use a screen reader, a magnifier, a braille display, voice control or switch access, you can tell us how
SightPress works with it before each release. Your experience matters more than any automatic test.

chunks.heading: Before each release
chunks.text:
Before each new version, we post a **Testers wanted** discussion on
[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/sightpress/core/discussions). It lists the new and changed screens, and how
to try them. Reply there to say you're taking part, or email <contribute@sightpress.org>.

chunks.heading: How to test
chunks.text:
1. Run SightPress on your own computer, as in [Getting started](../getting-started.md), and create a website.
2. Go through the screens listed in the discussion, with the technology you use every day, in the way you normally
   work. For example: sign in, write and publish a page, translate it, search the website, read the analytics.
3. Note anything that stops you, slows you down or surprises you: something not announced, announced twice or
   announced wrongly; focus that jumps or gets lost; a control you can't reach or operate; a chart or table you can't
   understand.
4. Note what worked well too. It tells us what to keep.

We test ourselves with NVDA and Firefox on Windows and VoiceOver and Safari on macOS. Other combinations, such as
JAWS, Narrator, TalkBack, VoiceOver on iOS, Orca, ZoomText or Dragon, are especially welcome.

chunks.heading: Report what you found
chunks.text:
For each problem, [report an accessibility barrier](report-a-problem.md): the task, your assistive technology and its
version, your browser and operating system, what happened and what you expected. Accessibility barriers are always
treated as bugs.

You never need to explain or prove a disability to take part.

The admin panel, the website screens (sign-in, search, error pages) and the emails can be translated. Each language
is one file. You need to be fluent in the language; you don't need to be a developer.

chunks.heading: What is translated today
chunks.text:
- **British English** (`en-GB`): the source language, and the language used when a text has no translation.
- **European Portuguese** (`pt-PT`) and **Spanish** (`es`): complete and reviewed.

Regional variants are separate languages: for example Brazilian Portuguese (`pt-BR`) is not European Portuguese, and
Latin American Spanish (`es-419`) is not Spanish from Spain.

chunks.heading: Translate into a new language, or fix a translation
chunks.text:
1. Download the source file,
   [messages.en-GB.xlf](https://github.com/sightpress/core/blob/main/resources/translations/messages.en-GB.xlf), and an
   existing translation as an example, such as
   [messages.es.xlf](https://github.com/sightpress/core/blob/main/resources/translations/messages.es.xlf).
2. Open it in a translation tool that reads XLIFF 2.0 files, such as Poedit, OmegaT or Virtaal, or in a text
   editor. Each text is a `<source>`; write your translation in the `<target>` next to it.
3. Keep the words in curly brackets, such as `{name}` or `{count}`, exactly as they are: SightPress puts a name or a
   number there. Keep any HTML such as `<strong>` too.
4. Use the words people use every day, as the English does. Short sentences are better than long ones.
5. Send the file:
    - by email to <contribute@sightpress.org>, saying which language it is; or
    - as a pull request to the [core repository](https://github.com/sightpress/core), if you know GitHub. The file
      goes in `resources/translations/messages.<code>.xlf`, for example `messages.fr.xlf`.

chunks.heading: What happens next
chunks.text:
- A second fluent speaker reviews every new language, and every new text, before it is released.
- Right-to-left languages, such as Arabic and Hebrew, also get a visual check of every screen.
- New texts that still need a review are marked `state="initial"` in the file. Reviewing them is a good first task.

Translating the documentation is not possible yet: it is written in British English only.
SightPress has a command line tool for tasks such as creating a website. This guide shows you how to run it.

chunks.heading: List the commands
chunks.text:
1. Open a terminal and go to the `skeleton` folder.
2. Type:

    ```sh
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress list
    ```

3. You should see a list of commands, each with one line about what it does, such as
   `site:create   Creates a site: its database, its first admin and its roles.`

chunks.heading: List your websites
chunks.text:
1. Type:

    ```sh
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:list
    ```

2. You should see one sentence for each website, with its status, its addresses, its language and its database. If
   you haven't created a website yet, it says "There are no sites yet. Create one with site:create."

chunks.heading: Get help with one command
chunks.text:
1. Type `help` and the name of the command, for example:

    ```sh
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress help site:create
    ```

2. You should see what the command needs and what each option means.

To create a website, see [Create a website](create-a-site.md). The [command line reference](../reference/command-line.md)
lists every command.

!!! tip "Shortcut for macOS and Linux"

    If the `make` program is installed, `make site-create NAME=demo` runs `site:create demo` and asks for the rest.

Some parts of SightPress are optional **features**, for example site search or visitor statistics. Each website has
its own: an admin can turn a feature off for one website and keep it on for the others. Turning a feature off hides
everything it adds, on the website and in the admin panel, and **keeps its data**, so turning it on again brings it
back as it was.

You need to be an **admin** of the website. Editors, contributors and members don't see the *Features* screen.

!!! note "Optional features in this version"

    This version of SightPress has three optional features of its own: **Site search** (see
    [Search your website](search-your-website.md)), **Analytics** (see
    [See who visits your website](see-who-visits-your-website.md)), both on for new websites, and the
    **AI assistant** (see [Use the AI assistant](use-the-ai-assistant.md)), off for new websites. Features installed
    as extra packages show up on the screen too.

chunks.heading: See the features of a website
chunks.text:
1. Sign in to the admin panel of the website, for example `http://localhost:8080/admin`.
2. In the admin menu, choose **Features**.
3. You should see one section for each optional feature, with its name as a heading, what it does, its **Status**
   ("On" or "Off") and what happens when it is off.

A feature that says **"set by your organisation"** was chosen for every website by whoever runs your SightPress
installation. It has no button, and it can't be changed from the website.

chunks.heading: Turn a feature off
chunks.text:
1. On the *Features* screen, find the feature and choose **Turn off** followed by its name, for example
   **Turn off Events**.
2. A page asks you to confirm and says what will happen. Choose **Turn off …** again to go ahead, or
   **Keep … on** to go back without changing anything.
3. You are back on the *Features* screen, at the feature's heading. A message at the top says that it is off and that
   its data is kept. Screen readers read the message out.
4. Check: the pages the feature added now answer "not found", and its screens have left the admin menu.

If another feature needs this one, SightPress refuses and names that feature: turn that one off first.

chunks.heading: Turn a feature on
chunks.text:
1. On the *Features* screen, choose **Turn on** followed by the feature's name.
2. You are back at the feature's heading, with the message "… is on."
3. Check: its pages and screens are back, with the data they had before.

If the feature needs another feature that is off, SightPress refuses and names the feature to turn on first.

chunks.heading: Delete a feature's data
chunks.text:
This removes everything the feature stored for the website, **for good**. You can only do it while the feature is off.

1. Turn the feature off (see above).
2. Under the feature, choose **Delete the data of …**. The link only appears when there is data to delete.
3. A page asks you to confirm. Choose **Delete the data of …** to go ahead, or **Keep the data** to go back.
4. The message says the data was deleted. Turning the feature on again later starts afresh, with no data.

Every change on this screen is written to the website's **Audit log**, with who made it and when.

chunks.heading: With the command line tool
chunks.text:
The same can be done in a terminal, in the `skeleton` folder. Replace `demo` with the short name of your website and
`acme.events` with the feature's id, which the first command shows.

1. List the features of a website and whether each one is on:

    ```sh
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:module:list demo
    ```

2. Turn one on, or off:

    ```sh
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:module:enable demo acme.events
    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:module:disable demo acme.events
    ```

3. Turn one off and delete its data for good:

    ```sh
